source.title: Universality and Hidden Information in Concept Bottleneck Models

record.file_problem: none; the full post is present, though referenced graphs are not reproduced with readable values in the text.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether independently trained models learn transferable, similar concept representations, using cross-model classification accuracy rather than a direct representation-similarity measure.
record.gate_note: The post reports cross-accuracy and cross-model transfer results, plus a source-classifier test of whether concept vectors reveal which model produced them. Referenced graph values are not available in the supplied text, so those results are recorded from the post's descriptions rather than inferred numerically. The concept-fidelity and species-classification results are not separately catalogued where they do not measure cross-model alignment.
record.test_reason: The post plugs one model's concept-bottleneck vectors directly into another model's classifier ('cross accuracy') to ask whether separately trained runs encode the same extra information the same way. This is a different method aimed at V3/V4, and it also bears on V7 (incomplete convergence, pretraining as cause). The ImageNet-pretrained Inceptionv3 backbone is shared across runs; only the concept and class heads are reinitialised, so 'different seeds' covers the heads only, except in the from-scratch test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author concludes that end-to-end CBMs hide extra information in the concept layer in very similar ways across runs. This is robust to head initialisation and fairly robust to dropout and loss weighting, but not to initialising the whole model, which suggests pretraining does much of the work. The hidden information goes mainly into low-entropy concepts. He draws implications for convergent steganography and its mitigation, and calls the results preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: Uses cross-model concept-vector classification and transfer in concept bottleneck models, rather than the original studies' representation-similarity methods. This is an Alignment Forum research post, not a replication.
record.method_sensitivity: Cross-accuracy changes with dropout and attribute-loss weight; the reported sharing differs between pretrained and from-scratch models.

fits_no_version.finding: Extra task information in joint CBMs is preferentially placed in low-entropy concepts; joint-vs-sequential deviation correlates negatively with label entropy, more strongly at higher attr_loss_weight.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In concept bottleneck models, hidden task-relevant information is encoded convergently in low-entropy concept channels.

record.problems: The author describes the work as ongoing and preliminary. It uses one dataset and principally one pretrained architecture; the from-scratch comparison has much lower validation performance and may not isolate the effect of pretraining. Many cross-accuracy results are presented only in graphs without values in the supplied text, and no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for species test performance or full-intervention performance: those assess task performance and concept fidelity rather than cross-model representation alignment. No separate row for the general observation that the mixed-source points lie on the frontier beyond r5.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep; one architecture.
Fully independent initialisation with good performance; other architectures and datasets; unit- or subspace-level matching.
Learned linear maps, stitching layers, relative representations, unpaired alignment; transfer across architectures.
No neuron, SAE or circuit comparison.
No variation of similarity metric or input distribution.
No plateau test; the role of pretraining is not isolated from model quality.

record.verdict_notes: LessWrong/Alignment Forum post, not an original source. All cross-accuracy results are figure-only with no numbers in the text; only the source-classifier table has values. The concept layer is supervised toward human labels, so part of the alignment is imposed. The interesting convergence is in the extra hidden information. The from-scratch comparison is confounded by far lower accuracy.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size or capability sweep, and no systematic comparison across different architectures, objectives, or datasets.
No vision-language model comparison or paired image-caption representations.
The study uses fine-tuned, ImageNet-pretrained Inceptionv3 models on one bird dataset; it does not test a range of architectures, tasks, or training stages.
Tests direct transfer of concept vectors between models, but not learned linear maps, layer stitching, relative representations, or transfer without paired data.
No comparison of recurring interpretable neurons, SAE features, or circuits across models.
Does not compare similarity metrics, their settings, or in-distribution and out-of-distribution inputs. It varies training settings, not convergence-measure settings.

The study reports incomplete transfer and differences across training conditions, and proposes pretraining as an explanation; it does not isolate shared data or objectives as causes, test a plateau, or compare a common-reality explanation directly.

rows.locator: Training Identical Models with Different Seeds; cross-accuracy graph
rows.note: The post says switching to crossed wires was barely noticeable in validation loss or accuracy. No graph values are available in the supplied text.
rows.check: State is right, but the subject should note that both runs start from the same pretrained Inceptionv3 weights and only the heads are reinitialised, so V3 is tested only for head initialisation. The value is figure-only.

rows.operation_detail: Compared cross-accuracy with one model's concept vectors generated with dropout.

conditions.value: 50% added before the separate concept-prediction heads in one model

rows.measure: Cross-accuracy relative to training accuracy and sequential-model performance
rows.baseline: training accuracy; sequential model on the same task
rows.value: figure only; text says cross-accuracy significantly lags training accuracy but remains far above sequential-model performance.
rows.note: The post also says dropout improved downstream performance when concepts were fully intervened on; that is concept-fidelity performance, not itself a cross-model alignment measure.
rows.check: OK. Cross-accuracy lags train accuracy but is far above the sequential baseline. Figure-only.

rows.subject: joint Concept Bottleneck Models with varied attribute-loss weights
rows.operation_detail: Compared cross-accuracy across models trained with different attribute-loss weights.

conditions.value: varied; graph includes models trained with different weights

rows.measure: Cross-accuracy when one model's concept vectors are classified by another model
rows.value: figure only; text reports low cross-accuracies for some differing weights, a smooth drop around the matching weight, a possible discrete shift between 0.5 and 1, and relatively stable encodings in the 2–5 range.
rows.note: The graph's individual values and exact pairwise conditions are not present in the supplied text. The post says the different weights can hide performance-boosting information in very different ways.
rows.check: Remove V3: varying attr_loss_weight changes the training objective, not the initialisation. Cross-accuracy is highest for matched weights and drops smoothly with mismatch; some pairs are low.

rows.subject: sequential concept-to-class model
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated the sequential classifier on concept vectors from joint models trained with varied attribute-loss weights.

conditions.value: joint models with varied attribute-loss weights

rows.measure: Class performance using concept vectors generated by other models
rows.baseline: sequential model using its corresponding concept vectors
rows.value: figure only; text says the sequential classifier performs better with joint models' concept vectors, including at low attribute-loss weights.
rows.note: This is a transfer result on the post's task, not a direct representation-similarity score.
rows.check: Remove V7. The sequential classifier, never trained on joint-model vectors, does better with them. This is transfer across objectives, not evidence about incompleteness or its causes.

rows.baseline: performance frontier from ordinary joint models

rows.locator: Training with the wires crossed; performance-frontier graph
rows.note: The post cautions that the classifier may distinguish the sources and learn different responses for them.
rows.check: Mixed-source training is scored on test/intervention performance frontiers, which cannot show cross-model alignment. The author notes the classifier may tell the sources apart.

relationships.reason: Convergence is incomplete: vector sources are distinguishable at 0.82–0.98 even for identical settings (r6–r9), and cross-accuracy lags (r2, r3). Sharing disappears without pretraining, which the author attributes to pretraining (r10, confounded).
relationships.display_finding: Vector sources remained distinguishable at 0.82–0.98 even under identical settings, and cross-model accuracy lagged; sharing disappeared without pretraining, although that comparison was confounded.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: Source classifiers achieve 0.823 and 0.981 accuracy for identical-setting pairs and 0.860 and 0.979 for differing loss weights. Transfer also depends on training settings; the from-scratch comparison suggests a pretraining contribution, with an explicit performance confound.
